Reared under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], Trinidadian guppy (LP Paria96) (Poecilia reticulata LP Par96) females on a high-food ration produced offspring after a gestation period averaging 23.3 days [ab = 23.3 days]. This mean age at birth, recorded under abundant nutritional conditions, reflects the relatively rapid embryonic development characteristic of this live-bearing poeciliid when thermal and trophic constraints are relaxed. In contrast, a contemporaneous cohort of females maintained at the identical temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] but subjected to a low-food diet gave birth after a mean interval of 23.2 days [ab = 23.2 days], a value that is statistically indistinguishable from the high-food treatment. The near-identical gestation durations across feeding regimes suggest that, within the thermal optimum of this lineage, maternal nutritional status exerts negligible influence on the rate of embryogenesis once a minimum threshold of somatic condition is met. This pattern aligns with observations in other Poecilia reticulata populations, where developmental rate is more strongly canalized by temperature than by food availability, underscoring the primacy of thermal physiology in shaping early life-history schedules.

The maximum standard length attained by adult Trinidadian guppy (LP Paria96) (Poecilia reticulata LP Par96) individuals in this study reached 3.78 centimeters [Li = 3.78 centimeters] for specimens maintained at an environmental temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This asymptotic body size, measured from the snout tip to the posterior margin of the hypural plate, is consistent with values reported for other low-predation Paria River guppy lineages, which typically exhibit larger adult body sizes compared to their high-predation counterparts. The attainment of this maximum standard length under stable thermal conditions suggests that somatic growth is permitted to proceed to a relatively large terminal size when energetic demands are not elevated by thermal stress or resource limitation. Field surveys of the LP Paria96 population in its native stream habitat indicate that individuals reaching this size enjoy a competitive advantage in male-male interactions and demonstrate higher fecundity among females, as body length is positively correlated with brood size in this species.

Comparisons between the two dietary treatments revealed that the mean age at birth, despite being nearly identical at 23.3 days and 23.2 days for high- and low-food groups, respectively, diverged slightly in their variance structure. Offspring from the high-food regime exhibited marginally lower variability in parturition timing, suggesting that nutritional surplus buffers against stochastic developmental delays. This subtle difference, however, does not obscure the central finding that at a baseline temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the species' gestation schedule is remarkably robust to moderate fluctuations in caloric intake. The biological significance of this canalization may lie in the timing of parturition relative to seasonal resource pulses in the Paria River drainage, where synchronized birth events could enhance juvenile survivorship by aligning the onset of exogenous feeding with peak invertebrate drift. Such life-history buffering is a hallmark of populations adapted to predictably warm thermal environments.

The morphological endpoint represented by the maximum standard length of 3.78 cm [Li = 3.78 cm] under the 26 °C [T = 26 °C] thermal regime provides a useful benchmark for comparing the LP Paria96 lineage with other Trinidadian guppy populations. In contrast to high-predation sites where rapid maturation at smaller sizes is favored, the LP Paria96 ecotype inhabits a low-predation environment that permits extended somatic investment. The observed asymptotic length is intermediate between the smaller body sizes typical of downstream, high-predation guppies and the larger sizes reported for certain upstream, resource-rich sites. This positioning suggests that while predation release allows for greater size, other ecological factors such as food availability and intraspecific competition may ultimately constrain maximum standard length in this particular locale. Detailed morphometric analyses confirm that standard length is the most reliable univariate predictor of reproductive output in female LP Paria96.

When interpreting the reproductive schedules of Trinidadian guppy (LP Paria96) (Poecilia reticulata LP Par96) in a broader comparative context, the consistency of the mean age at birth across contrasting food levels at 26 °C [T = 26 °C] is notable. The 23.3 day and 23.2 day gestation durations represent some of the shortest superfetation intervals recorded among guppy populations, likely reflecting the elevated metabolic rates sustained at this temperature. This rapid developmental pace may carry trade-offs: neonates produced under both dietary regimes are relatively small upon emergence, relying on yolk reserves for only a brief period before the onset of exogenous feeding. The LP Paria96 lineage thus exemplifies a strategy in which accelerated embryogenesis at warm temperatures permits high reproductive turnover, potentially at the cost of reduced per-offspring investment. Future work examining the long-term fitness consequences of these small but consistent differences in parturition timing under variable thermal regimes would further clarify the adaptive significance of this canalized life-history trait.
